newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SingTel aims for high growth despite competition.
newsitem.headline: SingTel aims for high growth despite competition.

text.p: Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SingTel) is aiming to maintain double-digit earnings growth despite fresh competition, senior officials said on Friday.
"Our management team is fully committed to try to maintain double-digit earnings growth," said Koh Boon Hwee, chairman of SingTel, Southeast Asia's biggest telecommunications group.
SingTel is facing tough competition from the entry of MobileOne in the cellular phone market in April, and from MobileOne and two other groups in the paging business.
In the year 2000 SingTel will also lose its monopoly on general telecommunications services in Singapore.

SingTel earlier on Friday announced net profit for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1997 grew 11.6 percent to Singapore $1.66 billion ($1.16 billion) on turnover of S$4.42 billion, in line with analysts' expectations.
Mano Sabnani, research director at DBS Investment Research, said he expected SingTel to deliver net earnings growth of 10 to 11 percent in fiscal 1998.

SingTel expects international direct dial (IDD) call volume to grow at double-digit rates but revenue growth would not match volume growth, Koh said. Revenue from international telephone services was seen growing at a slower pace in the current financial year as further IDD rate cuts were expected.
Revenue from international telephone services rose 5.2 percent in fiscal 1997 to S$1.9 billion.
On its cellular phone business, Koh said revenue was expected to grow but in the first year of competition, it might not match previous years' rates.
In fiscal 1997, SingTel recorded an 18.6 percent increase in revenue from mobile communications to S$759 million.
Lee Hsien Yang, SingTel's president and chief executive officer, added that costs in the cellular business would rise.
Koh earlier said that for fiscal 1998, SingTel's licence fee for mobile fees would rise to six percent of revenue of that business from 0.8 percent, costing the group S$20 million.
The performance of SingTel's associated companies had improved over the period.

Belgian telephone company Belgacom contributed S$111 million to SingTel, before taxes. SingTel, together with Ameritech Corp, Tele Danmark and three Belgian investors, holds a 49.9 percent stake in Belgacom. Lee said SingTel's share of of losses in associates Globe Telecom in the Philippines was S$21 million and in AAP Telecommunications in Australia was S$14 million.

On rumours that SingTel was taking a stake in PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia (PT Telkom), Koh said: "We can definitely say that Singapore Telecom has held no discussions with PT Telkom at this point in time," Koh said.
He added the group was looking at investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region, including Indonesia and China.
The group's cash balance as at the end of fiscal 1997 was S$4 billion, Koh added. (US$1=S$1.43)
